t: Maximum Sum Obtained of Any Permutation - Coverage Frequencies Meet the Rearrangement Inequality
o:
## Understanding the problem

After we permute nums, every request still sums over its fixed index range, and we maximize the grand total across all permutations. Permuting never changes which indices a request touches - only which values sit there - so the single thing that matters is how many requests cover each index. The optimum then falls out of the rearrangement inequality: pair the largest values with the most frequently covered indices.

For example 1, coverage of `[1,2,3,4,5]` under requests `[1,3],[0,1]` is `[1,2,1,1,0]`; pairing sorted-descending frequencies `[2,1,1,1,0]` with values `[5,4,3,2,1]` gives 10 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 0 = 19, matching the sample. Example 2 has one request over two indices: 6 + 5 = 11. Example 3 has coverages `[1,3,2,1,0,0]`, yielding 30 + 10 + 4 + 3 = 47.

With n and the number of requests up to 100000, painting each range naively costs O(n*q) and is too slow; a difference array recovers all coverages in O(n + q).
k: A permutation relocates values but never requests - each index's coverage count is invariant and fully determines the optimization.
Rearrangement inequality: sorting frequencies and values in the same order maximizes their dot product.
A difference array turns q range-increments into q point updates plus one linear prefix sweep.

a.i: Allocate a frequency array and, for every request, add one to each index it spans; then sort frequencies and values descending and sum the aligned products. The method is transparent and obviously correct, but any request may span all n indices, so the counting phase degrades to O(n*q) - far past the limits at n = q = 100000.
s: Initialize freq of size n to zero.
For each request [l, r], increment freq[i] for every i in [l, r].
Sort freq and nums in descending order.
Sum freq[i] * nums[i], taking the result modulo 1e9 + 7.
a.t: O(n*q + n log n) - each request paints its entire range.

a.i: Mark +1 at each range start and -1 just past each range end; one prefix sweep reconstructs exact coverage counts in linear time regardless of range lengths. Sorting both arrays and taking the dot product finishes via the rearrangement inequality. This classic trick replaces per-request range painting with two point updates.
s: Create diff of size n+1; for each [l, r] do diff[l] += 1 and diff[r+1] -= 1.
Prefix-sum diff into freq to recover per-index coverages.
Sort freq and nums in descending order.
a.t: O(n log n + q) - sorting dominates; each request costs two point updates.
a.sp: O(n) - the difference and frequency arrays.

w: Name the rearrangement inequality out loud in an interview - it is the crux of the problem, not the difference array. Pitfalls: an off-by-one on diff[r+1] when r equals n-1 (hence the size n+1 buffer), letting products overflow before taking the modulus in C++ or Java, and forgetting that uncovered indices must receive the smallest values rather than being skipped. Edge cases: no requests at all (answer 0), and a single request spanning the whole array. Likely follow-ups: minimize the total instead (pair ascending), support weighted requests, or answer queries online after the permutation is fixed.
